kurals.tamil:
அடக்கம் அமரருள் உய்க்கும் அடங்காமை
ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Adakkam amararul uykkum adangaamai
Aarirul uyththu vidum.
kurals.meaning: Self-restraint raises a person into the company of the gods; the lack of it drives him into a darkness so thick there is no escaping it.
kurals.elementary: Picture two staircases. One climbs up to a bright room full of wise, kind people; the other goes down into a dark basement with no lights. Every time you hold yourself back from doing something wrong, you climb one step up. Every time you just do whatever you feel like, you slip one step down.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by setting the stakes in the starkest possible terms: amarar (the immortals, the devas) versus aar-irul (a darkness that is ‘hard to bear’ or ‘dense’), which the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar glosses as a particular hell. Parimelazhagar defines adakkam as the condition in which body, speech and mind (mey, mozhi, manam) do not stray into wrong paths, and explains that the chapter follows ‘Impartiality’ because one who sees his own faults as clearly as others’ will naturally restrain himself. Modern commentators such as Karunanidhi read the couplet in this-worldly terms — restraint earns undying renown, indiscipline darkens life itself — showing how the couplet supports both a religious and a secular reading. Its two-path structure, one road upward and one downward, is among the most widespread forms in world ethical literature, from the Dhammapada’s ‘path to the Deathless’ to Paul’s sowing to the flesh or the Spirit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the unrestrained passions as the literal doorways into hell and tells Arjuna that a sensible person closes them.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita makes unrestraint the road into darkness, so restraint is what keeps a person out of it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the ‘unrestraint leads to hell’ half; the Gita verse does not state the upward ‘to the gods’ half explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes two harvests: indulging the flesh yields decay, while living by the Spirit yields eternal life.
christianity.tie_back: Same two destinations as the Kural: giving in to impulse leads down, disciplined living leads up to everlasting life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (two opposite destinies); ‘sowing to the Spirit’ is broader than self-restraint alone.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises Paradise to the one who restrains his soul from its unlawful desires out of awe of God.
islam.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s first line: holding back the self is what brings a person to the heavenly realm.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match on restraint of the self leading to paradise; the contrasting fate (Hellfire) appears in the preceding verses 79:37–39.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man’s pride shall bring him low; but he that is of a lowly spirit shall attain to honour.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that pride drags a person down while humility lifts him to honour.
judaism.tie_back: The same up-or-down outcome as the Kural, with humility (a core sense of adakkam) as the thing that raises a person.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the rise/fall structure and the humility sense of adakkam; the outcomes are worldly honour and abasement, not gods and hell.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents watchful self-guarding as the road to the Deathless (Nibbana) and careless living as the road to death.
buddhism.tie_back: Same two-road teaching: guarding oneself leads to the highest state, letting oneself go leads to ruin and darkness.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Appamada (heedfulness) overlaps heavily with adakkam but stresses vigilance more than humility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns his son Icarus to fly a middle course on their wax-and-feather wings. Icarus, thrilled by flight, soars too near the sun; the wax melts and he plunges into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows the fate of a youth who could not hold himself back from excess even when warned.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Icarus shows the Kural’s second line: lack of restraint doesn’t just fail, it sends a person plunging down.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the downward half vividly; there is no corresponding upward reward for restraint in the myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer driving a noble horse and an unruly one. Souls whose charioteer masters the unruly horse follow the gods up to the heavens and see true reality; those dragged about by it lose their wings and sink to earth.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the soul’s rise or fall depends on whether reason can govern appetite.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s myth has the same two directions as the Kural: self-mastery carries the soul up among the gods, unruliness drags it down.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel (ascent to the gods vs. fall), expressed as allegory rather than moral law.

kurals.tamil:
காக்க பொருளா அடக்கத்தை ஆக்கம்
அதனினூஉங் கில்லை உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaakka porulaa adakkaththai aakkam
Adhaninoovung killai uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: Guard self-restraint as you would guard a treasure, for no living being has any greater source of good than this.
kurals.elementary: People lock their money in a safe so nobody can take it. This kural says self-control is worth even more than money, so you should protect it just as carefully. You can lose toys or money, but if you hold on to your self-control, it keeps you good.
kurals.university: The key word is porulaa, ‘as wealth’ or ‘as a thing of real value’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as uruthip porul, an ultimate or assured good. The couplet turns ordinary economics upside down: restraint is not a sacrifice that costs us something but an asset (aakkam, ‘growth, prosperity’) that must be actively guarded (kaakka). That implies it can be lost or stolen, presumably by the passions. Parimelazhagar notes that uyir (‘living being’) here means human life in particular, since only humans can understand restraint and benefit from it. The idea that inner self-command is the truest possession has close relatives in the Stoic distinction between what is ‘up to us’ and what is not, and in the Mishnah’s redefinition of the mighty and the rich.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a disciplined mind lifts a person up while an undisciplined one drags him down, so one’s own mind is either best friend or worst enemy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat mastery over oneself as the greatest resource a person has, something to be protected and used for one’s own uplift.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘self-mastery is one’s greatest asset’ idea; the Gita doesn’t use the treasure metaphor.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sets the soul above the entire world’s wealth: nothing could be worth trading it for.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Jesus reorders what counts as ‘profit’: the inner life outweighs any outward gain.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel in value-reversal; the verse is about the soul generally, not self-restraint specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines real wealth as an inner state of contentment rather than an accumulation of things.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings move ‘wealth’ from outside to inside: a governed, satisfied soul is the true treasure.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on redefining wealth as an inner state; contentment is related to, but not identical with, restraint.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines might as self-conquest, and in the same teaching defines the rich man as ‘he who rejoices in his lot.’
judaism.tie_back: Just as Valluvar calls restraint the highest wealth, the Mishnah calls self-mastery true strength and contentment true riches.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit: self-conquest is recast as the highest possession and power.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wonderful, indeed, it is to subdue the mind, so difficult to subdue, ever swift, and seizing whatever it desires. A tamed mind brings happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the taming of the restless, grasping mind as the source of happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts name disciplining oneself as the single greatest good a person can obtain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct thematic match; ‘happiness’ stands where Valluvar has ‘aakkam’ (good, prosperity).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads, the young Heracles meets two women, Vice and Virtue. Vice offers an easy life of pleasure; Virtue tells him the gods grant nothing truly good without toil and discipline. Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable presents disciplined virtue as the path to real and lasting goods, and easy pleasure as a false bargain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles treats disciplined virtue as the treasure worth choosing above all, just as the Kural urges.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus’ ‘Choice of Heracles,’ in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21–34 (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shared valuation of self-discipline over pleasure; the treasure-guarding image is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Temperance, I replied, is the ordering or controlling of certain pleasures and desires; this is curiously enough implied in the saying of ‘a man being his own master’”
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines temperance (sophrosyne), one of the four cardinal virtues, as the well-ordered rule of the self over its desires.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato ranks self-mastery among the soul’s most precious possessions, much as Valluvar ranks restraint above all wealth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Defines the same virtue; Plato does not make the explicit ‘no greater gain’ claim here.

kurals.tamil:
செறிவறிந்து சீர்மை பயக்கும் அறிவறிந்து
ஆற்றின் அடங்கப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Serivarindhu seermai payakkum arivarindhu
Aatrin adangap perin.
kurals.meaning: If a person understands that restraint is itself wisdom and lives restrained in the right way, that restraint will be recognized by the good and will bring him distinction.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kid who quietly does the right thing in class without showing off. At first nobody seems to notice, but the teacher does, and soon everyone respects that kid. Quiet goodness gets noticed in the end.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on two uses of arindhu (‘having known’). In arivarindhu, the person first understands what true knowledge is; Parimelazhagar reads this as grasping that restraint itself is our wisdom. In serivarindhu, that restraint comes to be known and recognized, by the wise, in Parimelazhagar’s reading. The result is seermai, excellence or eminence. The qualifier aatrin (‘in the proper way’) rules out showy or grudging restraint. Manakkudavar adds a sensory reading: one must know the five sense-objects (taste, sight, touch, sound, smell) and restrain the five organs that seek them. Joining knowledge to restraint echoes the Delphic ‘Know thyself,’ which Greek thought tied to sophrosyne, and Aristotle’s view that the temperate person desires ‘as reason directs.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who restrains his senses, keeping them under full control, and fixes his consciousness upon Me, is known as a man of steady intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that sense-restraint is the mark by which a person of steady wisdom is known.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link restraint to wisdom and say it is what makes a person recognized as wise.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: restraint joined with wisdom and recognized as such; the Gita adds a devotional focus absent from the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:”
christianity.explanation: Peter promises that those who humble themselves will be lifted up at the proper time.
christianity.tie_back: Same arc as the Kural: restraint and humility practised now bring honour and distinction later.
christianity._accuracy_note: The exaltation comes from God rather than from recognition by the wise.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an identifies the true servants of God by their gentle bearing and restrained response to provocation.
islam.tie_back: Restrained conduct is what distinguishes these people and earns them their honoured title, much as the Kural says restraint brings distinction.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on restraint as a mark of distinction; the ‘knowledge’ element of the Kural is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth.”
judaism.explanation: When Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, the Torah records his exceptional humility, and God then publicly vindicates him.
judaism.tie_back: Moses’ restraint is noticed and honoured from on high, the same recognition the Kural promises to the restrained.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative parallel of humility recognized and vindicated; the verse itself states the trait, the vindication follows in 12:4–8.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the wise one with tamed senses and no pride is cherished even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts join wisdom with sense-restraint and humility and say such a person wins high regard.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: wisdom + restraint + no pride = esteem.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The maxims ‘Know thyself’ and ‘Nothing in excess’ were inscribed at Apollo’s temple at Delphi. In Plato’s Charmides, Critias argues that this self-knowledge is the very heart of sophrosyne (temperance).
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek religious tradition joined knowing oneself to keeping within limits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘knowing that restraint is wisdom’ matches the Delphic joining of self-knowledge and self-limitation.
greek_mythology.source: Delphic maxims, discussed in Plato, Charmides 164d–165a (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on knowledge-plus-restraint; the recognition/distinction theme is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the temperate man craves for the things he ought, as he ought, and when he ought; and this is what rational principle directs”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, temperance is desire rightly ordered by reason, neither suppressed blindly nor indulged.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘as he ought’ matches Valluvar’s aatrin, restraint practised in the proper way and guided by understanding.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.12, 1119b (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the reasoned, proper-mode restraint; Aristotle does not here speak of the resulting distinction.

kurals.tamil:
நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான் தோற்றம்
மலையினும் மாணப் பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilaiyin thiriyaadhu adangiyaan thotram
Malaiyinum maanap peridhu.
kurals.meaning: The stature of one who stays restrained, never swerving from his proper path in life, towers even higher than a mountain.
kurals.elementary: A mountain stays put no matter how hard the wind blows. A person who stays calm and humble and keeps doing the right thing, without bragging, looks even ‘taller’ to others than a mountain.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar reads nilai (‘station’) as the householder’s way of life, which fits the couplet’s place in the Illaraviyal (the section on domestic virtue). He takes ‘restraint without swerving’ to mean self-governance while still legitimately using the senses: disciplined participation in ordinary life, not ascetic withdrawal. Manakkudavar instead glosses nilai as one’s varnashrama duty. Thotram, ‘appearance’ or ‘stature,’ is read by Solomon Pappaiah as the impression such a person leaves in others’ minds, and the paradox is deliberate: the one who lowers himself appears the loftiest. The mountain works as an image of both height and immovability, which invites comparison with the Stoic promontory and the Buddhist unshaken rock.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna likens the steady sage to the ocean, which rivers keep pouring into without ever disturbing it.
hinduism.tie_back: Where Valluvar uses a mountain, the Gita uses the ocean: both picture the unswerving, restrained person as vast and unmoved.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel nature-image of immovable greatness; the Gita’s reward is peace rather than stature.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that self-exaltation leads to humiliation and humility to being raised up.
christianity.tie_back: The same paradox as the Kural: the one who holds himself low ends up standing highest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong paradox match; no mountain imagery or ‘unswerving station’ element.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an mocks arrogance: however proudly a person struts, he will never be as tall as the mountains.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an says arrogance can never reach a mountain’s height; the Kural says restraint rises above it. Both use the mountain to show that true greatness comes from humility.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking shared mountain image, used from the opposite (anti-pride) side.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; And he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks the self-controlled person above the warrior and the conqueror.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say self-rule gives a greatness beyond the world’s most impressive achievements, a conqueror’s in one case and a mountain’s height in the other.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in claim (self-mastery surpasses outward greatness); comparison object differs.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures the wise person as a solid rock that storms cannot move.
buddhism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s mountain, the rock stands for someone who stays steady and does not swerve from his course.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on immovability imagery; stresses equanimity more than humility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back home in disguise as a beggar, Odysseus is mocked by the suitors and the disloyal maids. Though his heart ‘growls’ within him, he tells it to endure, recalling that it once endured worse in the Cyclops’ cave, and holds himself back until the right moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero of the Odyssey shows restraint by refusing to strike prematurely, staying true to his purpose despite provocation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus stays restrained without swerving from his goal, and that restraint is exactly what makes his eventual victory so great.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of unswerving restraint; Odysseus’ restraint is strategic rather than humble.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to stand like a rocky headland that waves keep hitting without moving it.
philosophy.tie_back: Marcus’ unmoved promontory and Valluvar’s mountain are the same image: a steady, self-governed person standing tall above life’s turmoil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close image of unswerving firmness; ‘humility’ aspect not present.

kurals.tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல் அவருள்ளும்
செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து.
kurals._text_note: ytamizh.com and thirukural.ai read ‘செல்வம் தகைத்து’; thirukkural.com (with Parimelazhagar’s commentary) reads the sandhi form ‘செல்வந் தகைத்து’. Parimelazhagar notes the underlying form is ‘செல்வத்தகைத்து’. The meaning is identical in all three.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaarkkum nandraam panidhal avarullum
Selvarkke selvam thakaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Humility is good for everyone, but in the wealthy it shines as a second kind of wealth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid with the coolest new bike who still lets others ride it and never brags. Everyone likes that kid even more. Being humble when you have a lot is like having a bonus treasure on top of everything else.
kurals.university: Panidhal (‘bowing, humility’) makes explicit the social side of adakkam. Parimelazhagar explains why the rich are singled out: learning and noble birth already tend to restrain a person, so humility in the learned or well-born does not stand out, but wealth naturally breeds pride (perumitham). Humility in the rich is therefore especially striking, a ‘wealth added to wealth’ (selvam thakaiththu). He also points out that couplets 121–125 treat restraint in general, while 126 turns to bodily restraint, 127–129 to restraint of speech, and 130 to restraint of mind. The couplet reflects a view found in many traditions that prosperity, more than hardship, is the real test of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He, who is the master of riches but not of his senses, certainly loseth his riches in consequence of his want of mastery over his senses.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura warns King Dhritarashtra that wealth without self-mastery destroys itself.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura puts from the negative side what Valluvar puts positively: for the wealthy, restraint is what keeps and crowns their wealth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 34 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on the wealth–restraint link; speaks of sense-mastery rather than humility as such.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to warn the wealthy in particular against pride.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Paul singles out the rich as the people for whom humility matters most.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: humility specifically enjoined on the rich; lacks the ‘second wealth’ image.

islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that giving doesn’t diminish wealth and that humility raises a person’s standing.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings treat humility as an enrichment, something that adds to a person’s worth rather than taking away from it.
islam._accuracy_note: Places wealth and humility side by side and frames humility as gain; not addressed specifically to the rich.

judaism.quote_or_event: “and when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied; then thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity is exactly when pride and forgetfulness of God set in.
judaism.tie_back: Same insight as the Kural: wealth is the moment humility is most needed and most tested.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the danger of pride in prosperity; framed as warning rather than praise of the humble rich.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be respectful, humble, contented and grateful; and to listen to the Dhamma on due occasions — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In his list of life’s highest blessings, the Buddha includes humility.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha counts humility among life’s greatest blessings, close to Valluvar calling it a further wealth.
buddhism.source: Maha-mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Humility-as-blessing matches; there is no specific focus on the wealthy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The fabulously rich King Croesus of Lydia asks the Athenian sage Solon who is the happiest of men, expecting to be named. Solon refuses to call any man happy before his end. Later, defeated and on the pyre, Croesus remembers Solon’s words and calls out his name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition used Croesus as the classic case of a rich man whose pride is humbled by fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Croesus learns too late what the Kural teaches: in the rich, humility is the crowning quality and pride the fatal flaw.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Legendary-historical rather than strictly mythological; strong fit on wealth and the need for humility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These reasonings are unconnected: ‘I am richer than you, therefore I am better’; ‘I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better.’ … But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus points out the logical error in letting wealth inflate one’s sense of personal worth.
philosophy.tie_back: Epictetus shows why a rich person has no grounds for pride, which is why humility in the wealthy is the fitting response the Kural praises.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Directly addresses pride of wealth; argues from logic rather than praising humility as a further riches.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல் ஆற்றின்
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Orumaiyul aamaipol aindhadakkal aatrin
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: If, in this one life, a person can draw in his five senses the way a tortoise draws in its limbs, that power will guard him through seven births.
kurals.elementary: A turtle pulls its head and four legs into its shell when danger comes. We have five senses: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. If we can ‘pull them in’ when they want something harmful, we are protected just like the turtle in its shell.
kurals.university: The tortoise image (aamai) also appears in Bhagavad Gita 2.58 and in the Pali Kumma Sutta, which points to a shared South Asian stock of contemplative imagery rather than direct borrowing. Parimelazhagar explains the simile exactly: the tortoise withdraws its five members (four legs and head) so that harm cannot get in, and a person should restrain the five senses so that sin cannot get in. He classes this couplet as teaching bodily restraint (meyyadakkam). The contrast of orumai (‘one birth’) and ezhumai (‘seven births’) draws on karma doctrine: effort in one life gives a safeguard (emaappu, ‘protection, fortress’) across many lives, though Karunanidhi secularizes it as ‘for all time.’ The tortoise does not destroy its limbs; it withdraws and extends them at will, so the ideal is mastery of the senses, not mutilation of them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws its limbs within the shell, is firmly fixed in perfect consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna uses the very same tortoise image for the sage who can pull his senses back from their objects.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: the same animal, the same withdrawal of the senses, the same idea of protection through self-mastery.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of image and teaching; lacks the ‘seven births’ element.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes disciplining his body like an athlete so that he is not himself disqualified.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat mastering the body as a safeguard that protects a person’s ultimate destiny.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares bodily self-discipline as protection; no tortoise or five-senses imagery.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to guard their eyes and bodies as a means of purity.
islam.tie_back: Guarding the senses, like the tortoise guarding its limbs, keeps a person pure and protected.
islam._accuracy_note: Focuses on sight and chastity rather than all five senses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “that ye go not about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go astray;”
judaism.explanation: The commandment of the tzitzit (fringes) is given so that Israel will not be led astray by roaming heart and eyes.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the unrestrained senses as what lead a person astray, and reining them in as what protects.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on sense-restraint; the protective image is a garment-reminder rather than a shell.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a tortoise with its limbs withdrawn in its shell, so the monk, the thoughts of the heart.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Kumma Sutta, a tortoise keeps its four legs and neck withdrawn until a hungry jackal gives up; likewise Mara finds no opening in a monk whose sense-doors are guarded.
buddhism.tie_back: The same tortoise and the same five withdrawn members (four legs and neck) as in the Kural, with the same lesson: guard the senses and harm finds no way in.
buddhism.source: Kumma Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.199 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close: even the ‘five members’ (four limbs + neck) match Parimelazhagar’s gloss.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To pass the Sirens, whose song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so he cannot act on what he hears.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus survives by deliberately shutting off, or binding, his senses’ power to pull him toward destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the tortoise, Odysseus protects himself by pulling his senses back from a deadly attraction.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel of sense-restraint as safeguard; relies on external binding rather than inner mastery.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Philosophy, Socrates says, frees the soul by “persuading her to retire from them, and abstain from all but the necessary use of them, and be gathered up and collected into herself”
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedo, the philosopher draws the soul back from the deceptive senses into itself.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s soul ‘gathered into herself’ is almost the tortoise drawing into its shell: withdrawal from the senses as the path to safety and truth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match; Plato’s motive is epistemic (truth) as well as ethical.

kurals.tamil:
யாகாவா ராயினும் நாகாக்க காவாக்கால்
சோகாப்பர் சொல்லிழுக்குப் பட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaakaavaa raayinum naakaakka kaavaakkaal
Sokaappar sollizhukkup pattu.
kurals.meaning: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue; those who don’t will come to grief, caught in the faults of their own words.
kurals.elementary: If you can only remember one rule, remember this: watch what you say. A friend who blurts out a secret or says something mean in anger can lose friends in a second. Even if you mess up other things, keeping your words kind protects you.
kurals.university: The couplet performs its own lesson in sound: the syllable kaa (‘guard’) recurs in yaa-kaavaar, naa-kaakka, kaavaak-kaal and so-kaappar, which makes the verse itself an exercise in controlled, measured speech. Parimelazhagar treats sokaappar (‘they will grieve’) as a single verb, like allaappar, and reads yaa (‘whatever’) as meaning ‘all things without exception.’ This couplet opens the three-verse unit on restraint of speech (mozhi adakkam, 127–129). Its claim that the tongue ranks above every other thing needing guard is a striking priority that other traditions also make: the Hadith pairs the tongue with chastity as the key to Paradise, and the Epistle of James calls the untamed tongue a fire.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts disciplined speech as one of the three forms of austerity (tapas), alongside those of body and mind.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat control of the tongue as a spiritual discipline in its own right, not a mere nicety.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches speech-discipline; does not rank the tongue above all other restraints.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain.”
christianity.explanation: James says that all outward religion is empty if a person does not bridle his tongue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James makes guarding the tongue the one indispensable restraint, the test of all the rest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in priority; emphasizes the vanity of religion rather than personal suffering.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever can guarantee (the chastity of) what is between his two jaw-bones and what is between his two legs (i.e. his tongue and his private parts), I guarantee Paradise for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet singles out guarding the tongue (with chastity) as the key to Paradise.
islam.tie_back: Both texts pick out the tongue as the one thing a person above all must guard.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the tongue’s priority; pairs it with chastity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that guarding one’s speech protects one from trouble.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s point: guard the tongue, or suffer the troubles that loose speech brings.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both instruction and consequence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let a man guard himself against irritability in speech; let him be controlled in speech. Abandoning verbal misconduct, let him practice good conduct in speech.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to guard and control their speech and give up verbal misconduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use the language of ‘guarding’ speech and warn against faults of the tongue.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; part of a body–speech–mind triad that mirrors Parimelazhagar’s division of this chapter.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The best treasure a man can have is a sparing tongue, and the greatest pleasure, one that moves orderly; for if you speak evil, you yourself will soon be worse spoken of.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod, the poet of the Theogony, advises that a sparing, orderly tongue is a person’s greatest treasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod, like Valluvar, ranks the guarded tongue above other goods and warns that careless speech comes back on the speaker.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719–721 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Archaic Greek wisdom poetry rather than myth proper; the content match is very strong.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And let silence be the general rule, or let only what is necessary be said, and in few words.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus makes restraint of speech a basic rule of the Stoic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Both philosophers see a guarded tongue as the base of a disciplined life.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches speech-restraint; lacks the explicit warning of suffering from faulty speech.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்றானுந் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்
நன்றாகா தாகி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ondraanum theechchol porutpayan undaayin
Nandraakaa thaaki vidum.
kurals.meaning: If even a single harmful word causes harm through what it means, all the good a person has done turns to no good.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a big glass of milk with just one drop of poison in it. You can’t drink any of it now. In the same way, one really mean word can spoil lots of kind things you have said and done.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar identifies ‘evil words’ (theechchol) as falsehood, slander (kuralai) and harsh speech, and reads the couplet to mean that if even one harm reaches another person through such words, the good earned by all one’s other virtues is turned to evil. Manakkudavar offers a subtler alternative: even a single word that sounds sweet but carries a harmful meaning (porutpayan) makes the speech bad. Karunanidhi’s image of a drop of poison in a pot of milk captures the moral asymmetry: harm is not simply offset by good but contaminates it. That puts the Kural at odds with purely additive ‘merit ledgers’ and aligns it with Ecclesiastes’ dead flies in the perfumer’s ointment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Pride, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance – these qualities belong to those of demoniac nature, O son of Pṛthā.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita lists harshness of speech (parushyam) among the marks of a demonic nature.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat harsh speech as something that corrupts a person’s whole character, not a minor slip.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weaker match: condemns harsh speech but lacks the ‘one word spoils all good’ asymmetry. Best available Hindu parallel found.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be. Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?”
christianity.explanation: James says a mouth that both blesses and curses is as unnatural as a spring giving sweet and bitter water.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that bad words poison the good that comes from the same mouth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in the idea of mixed speech corrupting the whole; less explicit that one word cancels all merit.

islam.quote_or_event: “A slave (of Allah) may utter a word which pleases Allah without giving it much importance, and because of that Allah will raise him to degrees (of reward): a slave (of Allah) may utter a word (carelessly) which displeases Allah without thinking of its gravity and because of that he will be thrown into the Hell-Fire.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a single careless word can outweigh a person’s standing and cast him into the Fire.
islam.tie_back: Same asymmetry as the Kural: one evil word can overturn the good of a lifetime.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close in the ‘single word, total consequence’ logic.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Dead flies make the ointment of the perfumer fetid and putrid; so doth a little folly outweigh wisdom and honour.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes teaches that a small amount of folly can spoil a great store of wisdom and honour, just as dead flies ruin fine perfume.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the same image as Karunanidhi’s poison in milk: a small corruption spoils a large good.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact asymmetry; ‘folly’ is broader than harmful speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Surely, when a person is born, an axe is born in his mouth, with which he cuts himself— the fool saying a bad statement.”
buddhism.explanation: The monk Kokalika slanders the Buddha’s chief disciples Sariputta and Moggallana despite three warnings; though a monk, he falls into hell, and the Buddha speaks this verse.
buddhism.tie_back: Kokalika’s religious life counted for nothing once he spoke evil, which is exactly the Kural’s warning that one harmful word undoes all good.
buddhism.source: Kokalika Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.10 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative and doctrinal match on speech undoing merit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, a mortal so favoured that he dined at the table of the gods, is cast into eternal punishment. In Euripides’ Orestes, Electra says the cause was his ‘unbridled tongue,’ which she calls a most shameful disease.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this telling, a man who had every divine honour lost all of it through unrestrained speech.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus shows the Kural’s asymmetry: a lifetime of divine favour undone by a failure of the tongue.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Other versions of the myth blame different crimes (e.g., stealing ambrosia, serving Pelops); the ‘tongue’ version is Euripides’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “out of words light as air, in very deed the greatest enmities and hatreds spring up.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato forbids abusive speech because light words grow into the greatest enmities.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar both see that small, harmful words produce harm out of all proportion to their size.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches disproportionate harm of words; focuses on social enmity, not the cancelling of one’s own merit.

kurals.tamil:
தீயினாற் சுட்டபுண் உள்ளாறும் ஆறாதே
நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Theeyinaar suttapun ullaarum aaraadhe
Naavinaar sutta vadu.
kurals.meaning: A wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue never heals.
kurals.elementary: If you touch a hot stove, it hurts a lot, but in a week or two it heals. If someone says something really hurtful to you, you might remember it for years. Words can burn deeper than fire.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar notes Valluvar’s careful word choice: the fire-burn is called pun (a wound, which heals), while the tongue-burn is called vadu (a scar, which stays). He classifies the couplet as vetrumai alankaram, a figure of contrast: fire and harsh words share the act of burning, but because harsh words never heal they are shown to be worse than fire. The phrase ul aarum (‘heals within’) concedes that a fire-burn may leave an outward mark while the inner hurt fades; with verbal wounds the reverse holds. This is among the most widely quoted of all kurals, and its near-twin in the Mahabharata’s counsel of Vidura shows how old and widespread the insight is. Modern research on the lasting psychological effects of verbal abuse gives it contemporary resonance.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A forest pierced by arrows, or cut down by hatchets may again grow, but one’s heart wounded and censured by ill-spoken words never recovereth.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells Dhritarashtra that physical damage recovers but hearts wounded by harsh words never do.
hinduism.tie_back: The same structure as the Kural: physical harm heals, word-wounds do not.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 34 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel; arrows and axes stand where Valluvar has fire.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.”
christianity.explanation: James calls the tongue a fire that sets a person’s whole life ablaze.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts compare the tongue to fire, and both say its burning is worse than ordinary fire.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared fire metaphor; James stresses corruption of the speaker, the Kural stresses the victim’s unhealed scar.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to every scorner and mocker … It is the fire of Allah, [eternally] fueled, Which mounts directed at the hearts.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Humazah condemns the backbiter and mocker to a fire that reaches right into the heart.
islam.tie_back: The link is fire and hearts: in the Kural wounding words burn the victim’s heart, and in the Qur’an the mocker is repaid with a fire that reaches his own.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematic resonance only (verbal wounding and fire); the Qur’an describes retribution, not the permanence of the victim’s wound.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword; but the tongue of the wise is health.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares careless speech to sword-thrusts; the Talmud (Bava Metzia 58b) goes further, likening public humiliation to shedding blood.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat words as weapons that can wound as deeply as physical violence, or more.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on words-as-wounding; does not state the ‘never heals’ contrast.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that harsh speech wounds and brings painful consequences back on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts insist that harsh words really wound, so they must be held back.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the hurt of harsh words; lacks the fire/scar contrast and permanence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon publicly insults Achilles and takes his prize, Briseis. The dishonour sparks Achilles’ wrath, which lasts through most of the war and costs countless Achaean lives before he is finally reconciled.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad’s whole plot turns on a wound of words and dishonour that proves harder to heal than any battle wound.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles’ lasting wrath shows the Kural’s point: a verbal and public wound can outlast and outweigh physical injury.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The insult includes an act (seizing Briseis), not words alone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Anger may be defined as an impulse, accompanied by pain, to a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight directed without justification towards what concerns oneself or towards what concerns one’s friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle analyses how an unjust slight, often delivered in words, causes real pain and lasting resentment.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle explains the psychology behind the Kural: slights wound self-worth, which is why their pain lingers.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.2, 1378a (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Analytical rather than moral parallel; explains the wound but doesn’t compare it to fire or claim it never heals. Best available philosophical match found.

kurals.tamil:
கதங்காத்துக் கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான் செவ்வி
அறம்பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadhangaaththuk katradangal aatruvaan sevvi
Arampaarkkum aatrin nuzhaindhu.
kurals.meaning: Virtue itself enters the path of one who guards against anger, gains learning and is able to stay restrained, and waits there for the right moment to meet him.
kurals.elementary: Usually we have to go looking for good things. But if you learn a lot, stay calm when you’re angry, and stay humble, goodness comes looking for you, like a friend waiting at your door.
kurals.university: The closing couplet personifies Aram (Virtue; Parimelazhagar calls it ‘the deity of Dharma’) as a suitor who enters a person’s path and waits for his sevvi, the opportune moment when his mind, speech and face are gracious enough to be approached. This reverses the usual quest: instead of the seeker pursuing virtue, virtue pursues the restrained person. The condition has three parts: katham kaaththu (guarding against anger), katru (having learned) and adangal aatruvaan (being capable of restraint). Manakkudavar adds that the learned must also restrain the pride their learning can breed. Parimelazhagar classes this couplet as restraint of mind (manavadakkam), which completes the body–speech–mind triad around which the chapter’s second half is built. The pairing of anger control with learning parallels the Talmudic teaching that anger drives wisdom out of the sage.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Before giving up this present body, if one is able to tolerate the urges of the material senses and check the force of desire and anger, he is well situated and is happy in this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the one who checks the force of desire and anger is truly established and happy.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts promise that the one who masters anger will find the good (happiness, or virtue itself) coming to him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on anger-control bringing well-being; no personification of virtue seeking the person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that restraint in speech and anger opens the way to God’s righteousness, which human wrath cannot produce.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts link anger-restraint and readiness to learn (‘swift to hear’) with the arrival of righteousness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in its triad (hearing/learning, speech, anger) and outcome (righteousness).

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allah] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who restrain their anger and forgive, and says God loves them. A famous hadith (Bukhari 6114) adds that the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who restrains anger becomes the object of the good’s love and favour, rather than having to chase it.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: anger-restraint wins divine love; learning is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: Reish Lakish teaches that whoever becomes angry, if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him, and if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him, and he proves it from Moses, who forgot a law after becoming angry.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud warns that anger drives learning and prophecy out of even the greatest.
judaism.tie_back: The same pairing as the Kural: learning stays with the person who guards against anger and leaves the one who doesn’t.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on anger vs. learning, stated from the negative side; paraphrased from the Aramaic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says true mastery is checking anger the moment it rises.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make guarding against anger the defining mark of real self-mastery.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on anger-restraint; lacks the ‘virtue seeks him’ reward.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Achilles begins to draw his sword against Agamemnon, the goddess Athena comes down from heaven, seizes him by the hair and urges him to hold back. He obeys and sheathes the sword, and she promises him gifts three times as great later.
greek_mythology.explanation: A goddess personally comes to meet the hero at the very moment he restrains his anger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A striking echo of the Kural: when a man checks his anger, the divine comes to meet him on his path.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Athena arrives to prompt restraint rather than as its reward.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is angry at the right things and with the right people, and, further, as he ought, when he ought, and as long as he ought, is praised.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle praises the good-tempered person (praotes), whose anger is governed by reason.
philosophy.tie_back: Both see governed anger as a mark of virtue; Aristotle allows fitting anger, while Valluvar urges guarding against it altogether.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5, 1125b (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Partial: Aristotle endorses measured anger, the Kural counsels restraint of anger itself.
